claims.text: A multiscale approach can calculate lattice and electronic thermal conductivity as separate transport channels.
DFT-informed or machine-learned molecular dynamics can represent higher-order phonon dynamics for lattice-thermal-conductivity calculations.
Reliable interatomic parameters are required for the proposed molecular-dynamics treatment.
Electronic transport can be computed separately using an effective-medium or electron-scattering model and subsequently combined with the lattice contribution.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen reduces the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr by 20–30% relative to an oxygen-free alloy from 300 to 1200 K.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are nearly comparable.
Oxygen point defects create local lattice distortions and vibrational disorder in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-induced distortions act as phonon-scattering centers and increase phonon scattering rates.
Oxygen point defects do not directly affect the electronic transport channel.
Increased phonon scattering from oxygen selectively lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
Oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr has a lattice thermal conductivity approximately 20–30% higher than material containing about 1 wt.% oxygen.
The absolute lattice-conductivity difference between oxygen-free and oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr is roughly 5–10 W/(K·m).
Earlier Debye-temperature-based and defect-free analytical approaches overestimate thermal conductivity.
Earlier approaches conflate electronic and lattice thermal transport.
Explicitly modeling oxygen-induced atomic-scale imperfections will make the proposed approach more accurate than earlier approaches.
The quantitative predictions apply to powder-metallurgy HfNbTaTiZr with controlled oxygen levels over 300–1200 K.
Phonon-electron interactions make channel separation more uncertain near 200 K.
Variations in oxygen-defect distribution and processing conditions can change the magnitude of oxygen's thermal-conductivity effect.
Transport predictions for high-entropy alloys should be validated against experimental measurements.

contradictions.description: A 20–30% reduction relative to the oxygen-free value is not equivalent to saying that the oxygen-free value is 20–30% higher than the oxygen-contaminated value; the latter would be about 25–43% higher.

The boundary limits validity to 300–1200 K, but the hypothesis and predicted outcome also make a substantive prediction below 200 K. It is unclear whether the low-temperature result is within the claimed applicability domain or only an external benchmark.
